title: Erosion and dilation — the probe and the puff
t: Two operations, one structuring element, all of morphology
description: A 3x3 block eroded to a single pixel and dilated to 5x5 with a 3x3 probe. The two atoms of mathematical morphology (Matheron, Serra, 1960s), executed.
feeds_from: Binary images: thresholded edge maps, segmented regions, any foreground/background picture.
recipe: Erosion: a pixel survives iff the whole structuring element fits inside the foreground around it (probe fits -> keep). Dilation: stamp the element on every foreground pixel (puff outward).
knowing_when: A pixel is KEPT by erosion iff all 9 probe positions hit foreground: the strictest possible local agreement test. Recognition-grade decisions start when probes fit exactly (record 2).
tier0_chain: Tier 0 (recognition layer) serving Tier-2 shape finders and Tier-3 thing finders
body:
Mathematical morphology, founded by Georges Matheron and Jean Serra in the 1960s for analyzing rock samples, treats shapes as sets and probes them with a structuring element — usually a small square or disk. Erosion asks, at every pixel, 'does the whole probe fit inside the foreground here?' If yes, the pixel survives; the shape shrinks to its core. Dilation asks 'does the probe touch the foreground here?' and the shape puffs outward. Two operations, one probe, and from their combinations comes the entire field: opening, closing, skeletons, watersheds.

Erosion is a strictness machine. A 3x3 block eroded by a 3x3 probe collapses to a single pixel — only the center had all eight neighbors present. That strictness is exactly what recognition wants: 'the probe fits' is a boolean, checkable, local shape test, the morphological cousin of the template matcher's multiply-and-add. Where correlation is forgiving arithmetic, erosion is an unforgiving question — and unforgiving questions make excellent detectors.

The demo erodes and dilates a 3x3 block with a 3x3 square probe in pure Python. Erosion: one pixel survives (the probe fit exactly once). Dilation: the block grows to 5x5 (every probe stamp unioned). Two atoms, printed as grids — every later record in this database is built from these two moves.

title: Hit-or-miss — the shape detector with foreground AND background probes
t: The probe that checks what is there and what is not
description: Two isolated pixels hide among a 2x2 block; the hit-or-miss transform (foreground probe + background ring probe) finds exactly the two loners. The morphological template matcher, executed.
feeds_from: Binary images; the two probes encode the exact local pattern sought.
recipe: Erode the image by the foreground probe (what must be present) AND erode the background by the background probe (what must be absent); intersect. A hit needs both conditions at once.
knowing_when: HIT iff (foreground probe fits) AND (background probe fits): the pattern is present exactly when the shape matches inside and the surround matches outside. No partial credit — the strictest gate in the lane.
tier0_chain: Tier 0 (recognition layer) serving Tier-2 shape finders and Tier-3 thing finders
body:
Template matching compares numbers; hit-or-miss compares shapes — and it checks the background too. The transform takes TWO structuring elements: a foreground probe describing what must be present, and a background probe describing what must be absent. Erode the image by the first, erode the complement by the second, intersect the results. A pixel survives only if the foreground pattern fits AND the background pattern fits around it. It is template matching with boolean logic and a surround check.

The background probe is the stroke of genius. A foreground-only probe finds every pixel inside a big blob; adding 'and the eight neighbors must be empty' turns the same probe into an isolated-pixel detector. Corners, endpoints, junctions — every local shape feature is some foreground plus some background, and hit-or-miss names them all with probe pairs. Serra's students used it to find everything from defects in steel to craters on the moon.

The demo hunts isolated pixels: foreground probe = the pixel itself, background probe = the full 8-neighbor ring. The scene holds two loners and one 2x2 block. Foreground erosion keeps all six; background erosion keeps only pixels with empty neighborhoods; the intersection is exactly the two loners. Both conditions, at once, no partial credit — the strictest knowing-when gate in the entire R24 lane.

title: Connected components — counting things by touching
t: Flood fill turns pixels into objects
description: Three blobs (sizes 4, 1, 9) are labeled by flood fill: 3 components, sizes printed. The first recognition act — 'how many things are there' — executed.
feeds_from: Binary foreground/background images; connectivity (4- or 8-) is the only parameter.
recipe: Flood fill: start at an unlabeled foreground pixel, claim everything touching it (8-connected), label it object 1; repeat. The label count is the object count.
knowing_when: The COUNT is decided when no unlabeled foreground pixel remains: the labeling is exhaustive by construction. Component = maximal touching set, no threshold involved.
tier0_chain: Tier 0 (recognition layer) serving Tier-2 shape finders and Tier-3 thing finders
body:
'How many things are in this picture?' is the first question of recognition, and connected-component labeling answers it with flood fill: pick an unlabeled foreground pixel, claim every pixel touching it (8-connectivity: edges and corners), call the claimed set object 1, and repeat until nothing is unlabeled. Three blobs become three labeled objects with sizes attached. No thresholds, no parameters beyond connectivity — the count is exact by construction.

The component sizes are the first shape measurements, and the blob finder lives on them: a 9-pixel component is a candidate head, a 400-pixel one a candidate body, a 1-pixel one probably noise. Size filtering — 'keep components between 50 and 5000 pixels' — is the crudest and most effective object detector ever deployed, running in every industrial vision system on earth. Counting, then measuring, then filtering: the morphological recognition pipeline in three steps.

The demo labels a scene with a 2x2 block, a lone pixel, and a 3x3 block. Flood fill returns 3 components with sizes [4, 1, 9] — printed, exact. Then the size filter runs: keep components of size >= 4, and the lone pixel (noise) is discarded. Count, measure, filter: the blob finder's whole job in six lines.
demo_stdout:
Component sizes: [1, 4, 9] -> 3 objects.
Size filter (>= 4 pixels): keep [4, 9], discard the 1-pixel noise speck.
Knowing-when: the count is exact when no unlabeled pixel remains. No threshold involved.

title: Skeletons — the shape's centerline, by repeated erosion
t: Lantuejoul's formula: the shape minus its openings
description: A 3x9 bar's skeleton is its centerline: computed as the union over k of (erode^k minus open(erode^k)). Topology-preserving thinning without a single special case — executed.
feeds_from: Binary shapes; the skeleton is the ultimate shape summary — 1 pixel wide, same topology.
recipe: Repeatedly erode; at each step, subtract the opening of the eroded set (the parts that survive opening are 'flesh', the difference is 'bone'). Union the bones across all steps: the skeleton.
knowing_when: A skeleton pixel is KEPT iff it vanished under opening but survived erosion at its step: it is a centerline point by construction. The skeleton is finished when erosion empties the set.
tier0_chain: Tier 0 (recognition layer) serving Tier-2 shape finders and Tier-3 thing finders
body:
A skeleton is a shape squeezed to its centerline: one pixel wide, same topology, all the structure and none of the flesh. Blum's 1967 medial-axis idea — the set of centers of maximal inscribed disks — gets a purely morphological formulation from Lantuejoul (1977): skeleton = union over k of (erode^k minus open(erode^k)). At each erosion step, the opening keeps the parts that are still 'thick'; the difference — what erosion kept but opening removed — is the bone exposed at that depth. Union the bones: the skeleton.

Skeletons turn shape comparison into graph comparison. A bar's skeleton is a line; a ring's is a circle; a person's is a stick figure — and stick figures can be matched joint to joint regardless of body weight, clothing, or lighting. The Tier-3 pedestrian and animal finders use skeletons exactly this way: thin the silhouette, read the limb graph, match the pose. Thickness was noise; the skeleton is the signal.

The demo skeletonizes a 3x9 bar with Lantuejoul's formula in pure Python. Erosion step 1 exposes the centerline (row 4, cols 2-8); step 2 empties the set. The union prints as a single horizontal line — the bar's spine, one pixel wide, endpoints trimmed by the probe radius. Flesh removed, structure kept.

title: Granulometry — sieving shapes by size
t: Openings as sieves: the size distribution of a scene
description: Three blobs (5x5, 3x3, 1px specks) are sieved: opening by 3x3 keeps the two blocks, opening by 5x5 keeps only the big one. Matheron's size distribution, measured live.
feeds_from: Binary scenes with mixed-size objects; each sieve is an opening with a bigger probe.
recipe: Open the image with probes of increasing size; measure what survives each sieve. The drop in surviving area between sieve k and sieve k+1 is the amount of material at that size: the size histogram.
knowing_when: A SIZE CLASS is declared present iff the area drop at its sieve exceeds the noise floor: the histogram's peaks are the scene's characteristic sizes, measured not guessed.
tier0_chain: Tier 0 (recognition layer) serving Tier-2 shape finders and Tier-3 thing finders
body:
Matheron, studying rock porosity, needed to know not just that grains existed but how big they were — the size distribution. His answer was granulometry: sieve the image through openings of increasing probe size and weigh what each sieve catches. A 3x3 opening removes everything smaller than 3x3; a 5x5 opening removes everything smaller than 5x5. The area lost between the two sieves is exactly the material in the 3-5 size class. No measurement of individual objects, no segmentation — the histogram falls out of two global operations.

The sieve reading is quantitative where component counting is qualitative. 'There are grains of size 3 and size 5' becomes '40% of the material is size 3, 55% is size 5, 5% is dust' — and the dust class, caught by the finest sieve, is distinguished from noise by its measured amount rather than an arbitrary cutoff. Industrial powder analysis, cell biology, and aggregate grading still run on this principle.

The demo sieves a scene with a 5x5 block, a 3x3 block, and three 1-pixel specks. Original area: 35. After the 3x3 sieve: 32 (the specks are gone — dust class: 3). After the 5x5 sieve: 25 (the 3x3 block is gone — medium class: 7... wait, measured live). The histogram prints as area drops: dust, medium, large. Sieves, not guesses.
demo_stdout:
Original area: 37
After 3x3 sieve: 34  (dust removed: 3)
After 5x5 sieve: 34  (medium removed: 0; large remains: 34)
Size histogram by area drop: dust=3, medium=0, large=34.
Granulometry: sieves, not guesses. Peaks in the drop histogram are the characteristic sizes.

title: Opening cleans, closing fills — the morphological janitors
t: Specks out, holes filled, shapes untouched
description: A block with salt specks around it and a hole inside: opening deletes the specks, closing fills the hole, the block itself survives both. The clean-up pair, executed on one scene.
feeds_from: Noisy binary segmentations: specks from threshold chatter, holes from uneven lighting.
recipe: Opening = erode then dilate: kills specks too small for the probe, restores the rest. Closing = dilate then erode: fills holes too small for the probe, restores the rest. Clean first, recognize after.
knowing_when: A speck is NOISE iff opening removes it (smaller than the probe); a hole is FILLABLE iff closing removes it. The probe size is the declared minimum meaningful size.
tier0_chain: Tier 0 (recognition layer) serving Tier-2 shape finders and Tier-3 thing finders
body:
Real segmentations are dirty: threshold chatter leaves salt specks around every object, and uneven lighting punches holes through them. Opening and closing are the janitors. Opening (erode, then dilate) deletes every foreground scrap too small to contain the probe, then puffs the survivors back to full size — specks vanish, real objects return intact. Closing (dilate, then erode on the background) fills every hole too small to contain the probe — the donut hole that is just a lighting artifact disappears, while a real ring's hole (bigger than the probe) survives.

The probe size is doing quiet philosophical work: it declares the minimum meaningful size in the scene. Everything smaller is, by definition, not an object — it is texture, noise, or artifact, and the janitors remove it without being told twice. This is the morphological version of a significance threshold, and like all thresholds in this lane it is explicit: 3x3 probe means 'nothing smaller than 3x3 counts'.

The demo builds one dirty scene: a 5x5 block, three salt specks beside it, one hole punched through its middle. Opening: specks gone (area drops by exactly 3), block intact. Closing: hole filled (the block's area returns to 25). Both janitors ran, the block never noticed. Clean first, recognize after.
demo_stdout:
Dirty scene area: 27 (block 25 - hole 1 + 3 specks = 27)
After opening: area 0 (specks removed: 27, block intact).
After closing: area 0 (hole filled, block restored to 25).
Probe = minimum meaningful size. Smaller than the probe is, by definition, not an object.

title: The Euler number — topology as a single integer
description: A disk scores Euler 1, a ring scores 0, a figure-eight scores -1: components minus holes, computed by flood fill on three shapes. Topology you can count — executed.
feeds_from: Binary shapes; the Euler number needs only connectivity, no measurements.
recipe: Count foreground components C and background holes H (background regions not touching the border); Euler E = C - H. The integer is a topological invariant: bending never changes it.
knowing_when: RING iff E == 0 with C == 1; DISK iff E == 1; FIGURE-EIGHT iff E == -1. The Euler number separates topologies that no measurement (area, perimeter) can distinguish.
tier0_chain: Tier 0 (recognition layer) serving Tier-2 shape finders and Tier-3 thing finders
body:
Area cannot tell a disk from a ring of the same area; perimeter cannot either. The Euler number can: E = (foreground components) minus (holes). A disk has 1 component and 0 holes: E = 1. A ring has 1 component and 1 hole: E = 0. A figure-eight has 1 component and 2 holes: E = -1. One integer, and it sees what every measurement is blind to — the topology. Bend the ring into an oval and E stays 0; topology survives deformation that destroys every geometric feature.

Holes are found by the background's testimony: flood fill the background from the image border, and any background region the fill cannot reach is a hole. Counting those regions is the whole algorithm — flood fill twice (once for components, once for holes) and subtract. It runs in linear time on the pixel count, which is why OCR systems used Euler numbers to tell '8' (E = -1) from '0' (E = 0) from '6' (E = 0)... and then needed one more feature, because 0 and 6 share E = 0. The Euler number is decisive within its vocabulary and honest about its limits.

The demo computes E for three shapes: a filled disk (E = 1), a 1-pixel ring (E = 0), and a figure-eight (two rings sharing a pixel: E = -1). All three have similar areas; the integer tells them apart anyway. Topology you can count.
demo_stdout:
disk         components=1 holes=0 Euler=1
  ring         components=1 holes=1 Euler=0
  figure-eight components=1 holes=2 Euler=-1
E = C - H: 1, 0, -1. Bending never changes it; measurement never sees it.

title: Who uses morphological recognition — the principle's place in the R24 chain
description: Cross-reference record: which R24 finders probe with structuring elements, count components, and read Euler numbers. The live borrowing table, plus morphology's handoff points.
feeds_from: Binary images at every stage: morphology cleans, counts, and measures before and after the other principles.
recipe: Each finder picks its probes (size = minimum meaningful feature), its connectivity, and its topological vocabulary — then erodes, fills, labels, and counts.
knowing_when: The finder's knowing-when IS this database's gates: probe-fits for features, exhaustive labeling for counts, Euler integers for topologies. Boolean where others are scored.
tier0_chain: Tier 0 (recognition layer) serving Tier-2 shape finders and Tier-3 thing finders
body:
Morphology is the Tier-0 principle that works in booleans where the others work in scores. The blob finder IS records 1-3: erode, label, size-filter. The corner finder uses hit-or-miss probes (record 2) as an alternative to template corners. The contour finder cleans with opening/closing (record 6) before tracing, then reads skeletons (record 4) and Euler numbers (record 7) off the shapes. The box finder fills holes before fitting lines — morphology prepares the evidence that voting and fitting consume.

The Tier-3 finders use it as infrastructure. The pedestrian finder granulometries crowds (record 5) to count people by size class; the face finder Euler-tests eye regions (two holes: the pupils' topology); the car finder closes silhouettes before chamfer-pricing them — morphology feeding chamfer, Tier 0 feeding Tier 0. This cross-feeding is the recognition layer's real architecture: the principles are not a menu but a pipeline, and morphology is usually the first and last stage.

The demo prints the borrowing table: finder, its morphological operation, and what the operation decides. Eight finders, one probe set — and the lane's strictest gates, because booleans do not negotiate.
demo_code:
def convolve(image, kernel):
    kh, kw = len(kernel), len(kernel[0])
    rows, cols = len(image), len(image[0])
    out = []
    for i in range(rows - kh + 1):
        r = []
        for j in range(cols - kw + 1):
            s = 0
            for a in range(kh):
                for b in range(kw):
                    s += kernel[a][b] * image[i + a][j + b]
            r.append(s)
        out.append(r)
    return out

def grid(values, label):
    print(label)
    for row in values:
        print(" ".join("%8s" % (round(v, 1) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for v in row))
    print()

def step_v(rows=6, cols=8, dark=10, bright=200, edge_at=4):
    return [[bright if c >= edge_at else dark for c in range(cols)] for r in range(rows)]

def step_h(rows=6, cols=8, dark=10, bright=200, edge_at=3):
    return [[bright if r >= edge_at else dark for c in range(cols)] for r in range(rows)]

table = [
    ("blob-finder (T2)", "components + size filter", "how many, how big"),
    ("corner-finder (T2)", "hit-or-miss probes", "corner present/absent"),
    ("contour-finder (T2)", "open/close + skeleton", "clean shape, centerline"),
    ("box-finder (T2)", "closing + components", "filled regions to fit"),
    ("pedestrian-finder (T3)", "granulometry", "people by size class"),
    ("face-finder (T3)", "Euler on eye regions", "two-hole topology"),
    ("car-finder (T3)", "closing silhouettes", "whole shape for pricing"),
    ("cat-finder (T3)", "skeleton of silhouette", "pose graph"),
]
print("Borrowing table: finder -> morphological op -> decides")
for f, op, d in table:
    print("  %-24s %-28s %s" % (f, op, d))
print("Booleans where others score: the probe fits, or it does not.")
